author: Dilantha De Silva
title: 6 Portfolio Allocation Strategies For 2019
text:
Overview 2018 marked the worst year for U.S. stocks in over a decade, with all the major indexes down for the year, despite the promising performance in the middle of the year. A number of reasons contributed to the downfall of U.S. stock markets and global markets followed suit.
Global market performance in 2018
(Source - Author prepared based on Morningstar data)
There was a bloodbath in bond markets as well, triggered by rising rates. Among other reasons, a flattening yield curve, slowdown in economic growth, trade tensions, and Fed rate hikes contributed to this overall market decline. Moving onto 2019, investors need to factor in developing macroeconomic trends to avoid being exposed to the risk of significant losses and identify opportunities that will yield the most. This analysis begins with identifying the current stage of the market and expands into identifying investment opportunities for 2019, along with certain strategies that would reduce the overall risk of the portfolio and help investors achieve optimal returns on capital invested.
Current stage of the bull market The current bull market has lasted nearly a decade, and on the 22nd August 2018, many investment firms and media outlets announced that this is longest-running bull market since World War II.
While investors were keen to question whether this is indeed the longest-running bull market or not, the real problem back then was whether this bull market was going to last much longer.
Bull days as of 08/21/2018
(Source - CNBC )
Even though markets have continued to rally for almost 10 years, since September last year, stocks have declined significantly, including the drivers of the market since 2016, such as Facebook (NASDAQ: FB ), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), Netflix (NASDAQ: NFLX ), Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN ), and Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ). With this, the Shiller P/E ratio has come down from the highs seen in early September last year.
(Source - Multpl )
This all-important indicator is trading well below the absurd highs of financial crisis but has continued to ascend at a steady pace, as investors have felt more at ease to assume a much higher level of risk, in line with expected double-digit growth rates.
There is an ongoing debate on the expected growth rate of earnings per share (EPS) of public companies in the U.S., and numerous reports were released by major investment banks, brokerage houses, and equity research firms citing that corporate profits are at its peak . Understandably, if earnings growth decelerates, stocks would suddenly be considered a much more risky asset to invest in, and this would lead to another bloodbath in equity markets around the world.
Despite the historic run in markets, I believe prudent investors still can find undervalued issues, which are expected to provide significant returns to investors, as stock prices converge with their respective intrinsic values. However, stocks that are trading at rich multiples might continue to hurt investors in 2019, as growth prospects diminish.
Timing markets are something that investors should avoid at all costs, as it would be impossible to time markets correctly, regardless of the breadth of knowledge and experience one might have. Therefore, I believe investors should continue to focus on underlying fundamentals to find attractive stocks and other investment opportunities. The market is certainly in the late stage of this bull cycle, but as long as investors remain focused on fundamentals, attractive investment opportunities can be unveiled in 2019.
Investment strategies for 2019 Value stocks over growth stocks
Over the last 10 years, growth stocks have significantly outperformed value stocks, supported by low interest rates, exceptional growth in e-commerce, and the rise of information technology.
Russell 1000 Growth vs. Russell 1000 Value performance
(Source - Yahoo Finance)
Evidently, the Russell 1000 Growth Index has gained 272% since 2009, whereas the Russell 1000 Value Index has returned only 156%. Historical performance is, of course, not a reliable indicator of future performance, and I believe things are starting to look good for value stocks but not so much for growth stocks.
The Russell 1000 Growth Index trades at a P/E of 24.4 times , whereas the Russell 1000 Value index trades at a P/E of just 17 times . If we factor in the expected decline in corporate earnings, growth stocks would be hurt the most, as these are already trading at much higher valuation multiples.
Historically, value stocks have outperformed growth stocks when interest rates were rising, which exactly is the case now. Jonathan Lewellen, a finance professor at Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth, looked at rising rate environments since 1983 and concluded the below.
The short answer is that value stocks seem to outperform growth stocks during periods when the federal funds rate is increasing, mostly because growth stocks do relatively poorly. However, growth stocks have historically performed well in the 06 months leading up to rate increases." - Jonathan Lewellen
Growth stocks are sensitive to interest rate hikes, as these companies assume a significant amount of debt to support their growth operations. In addition, banks and industrial companies generally represent the value sector, and these sectors are the least affected when rates rise. Moreover, as growth stocks are valued based on future expected earnings, a rate hike can be particularly seen as an obstacle, whereas value stocks are usually valued based on their current and historical earnings.
Interest rates are poised for further hikes in 2019, and along with it comes the risk of a possible slowdown in economic activities, which are all ominous signs for growth stocks. Investors need not panic though but be a little cautious when investing in growth stocks. Actionable advice would be to reassess portfolio holdings and focus shift to a more value-oriented approach when investing in stocks, in 2019.
Dividend investing
As we move on to a possibly volatile year for stocks across the globe, investors would be better off emphasizing on the income portion of their portfolios. With this in mind, a strategic portfolio allocation toward dividend-paying stocks is encouraged.
Even though dividends form an important portion of return to investors, recent capital gains in technology and energy sector stocks have prompted many investors to choose growth stocks over dividend-paying stocks.
(Source - Sure Dividend )
However, I believe 2019 is a year, in which, investors should focus more on accumulating income from dividends. With the recent market downturn, many dividend aristocrats have plummeted, providing a great opportunity for investors to buy these high dividend-paying stocks at a bargain, which will boost the income portion of the portfolio. Dividends are a hedge against capital losses as well, and at the same time, dividends can be the difference between a successful and unsuccessful portfolio, at times of market crises.
While the S&P 500 dividend yield is nowhere near historical highs, the yield has improved during the last couple of months, as markets pulled back.
S&P 500 dividend yield
(Source - Multpl)
Even though the S&P 500 dividend yield is 2.07%, a handful of safe dividend-paying companies are now trading with yields above 5%, which should be another incentive for investors to consider dividend investing.
Maintaining a healthy cash balance
Market volatility has returned once again, and investors can expect to see drastic changes in stock prices, within a limited period of time. As it always happens in volatile markets, undervalued picks will momentarily trade at bargain prices, and investors need to be ready to make the most of such opportunities. While such a strategy might seem bearish at first sight, this is the exact root of opportunistic investing.
In my opinion, 2019 will bring many such opportunities to investors, as trade talks continue to swivel from one end to the other, and the Fed keeps on hiking rates to cool down the economy. Maintaining a sufficient cash balance in the portfolio makes sense, as market volatility is expected to increase in 2019.
Investors have a few options to choose from, to hold their investable cash until an opportunity presents itself.
Money market funds Checking accounts Treasury securities Short-term certificates of deposits Inflation-linked savings deposits/bonds Investing globally
U.S. markets significantly outperformed world markets in 2018, driven by various reasons including steady earnings growth, appreciation of the U.S. dollar, the trade war situation, and political uncertainty in emerging countries.
While most emerging markets entered bear market territory in 2018, their currencies took a major hit as well, as the Fed continued to hike rates in the U.S. The massive debt pile of emerging markets was once again put to test, which became too much of a burden for many institutional investors, who were keen to seek alternatives to emerging markets.
(Source - Yardeni Research)
On the back of a rough 2018, emerging markets are trading at much more attractive valuation levels at present. Investors need to embrace a few economic developments, such as the rise of India and Brazil when deciding on the optimal portfolio allocation.
(Source - The Economist )
Prudent investors can get exposure to growing markets by using American Depository Receipts (ADRs) or index funds.
European stocks have underperformed U.S. stocks for an extended time period as well, and more recently, European equity markets tumbled as political stability in few European countries came into question.
(Source - Bloomberg)
These political uncertainties will continue to prevail in 2019, but we can continue to search for catalysts that would unlock value in the future.
China markets have also entered bear territory, which presents another opportunity for investors to consider investment opportunities in China. For an example, the Shanghai Composite trades at a P/E of 12 and the Hang Seng Index trades at a PE ratio of 10 .
Despite attractive valuation levels in European and Asian markets, investors need to consider growth opportunities and available catalysts, before investing in these markets. However, in 2019, it would be worthwhile to consider allocating a portion of portfolio to these markets, as we can expect a major rally if the dollar depreciates against other currencies and the Fed pauses tightening the monetary policy.
Gold as a potential hedge against market downturns
Gold remains one of the most accepted forms of hedges against stock market crashes, for good reasons. Historically, gold has negatively correlated with stock prices, during times of financial crises. Even though we are not predicting an economic recession or a financial market crisis in 2019, investors need to be prepared and know their options. While there are arguments for and against using Bitcoin as a hedge for stock market downturns, I believe investors should focus on using gold as a hedge, which is a tried and tested method.
A research done by Trinity College found that gold is the best hedge against a potential stock market crash.
(Source - Market Realist )
The focus here should be not on identifying whether gold has shown a negative correlation to stock prices when stock prices were moving higher, but rather, on identifying whether gold has remained stable or rallied higher when stock prices were declining.
During the financial crisis and dotcom bubble, gold prices continued to move higher, while stocks tanked, which is proof of how gold has successfully acted as a hedge against stock market downturns.
While we do not need to expose ourselves to gold in a significant way, it would be better to invest a small portion of funds in gold, possibly via an exchange-traded fund (ETF), and in other commodities, as commodities have historically been natural hedges against drastic stock market downturns.
Diversification
Diversification will play a key role in the success of our portfolio in 2019. During the last couple of years, risk-seeking investors were fully invested in stocks; mostly technological stocks and were still able to realize nice returns, despite a significant lack of diversification. However, in 2019, I believe such a strategy exposes investors to the risk of massive capital losses, as markets will continue to be volatile and unpredictable.
How to build a diversified portfolio in 2019?
Allocate a portion of the portfolio to fixed income securities, such as U.S. Treasury bonds Invest in a wide range of sectors, including technology, healthcare, automotive, utilities, consumer discretionary and consumer cyclical Invest globally Model portfolio allocation In line with the above strategies discussed, I have prepared the below portfolio allocation model to help me invest in 2019. As emphasized above, diversification will play a key role in the success of our portfolio performance in 2019.

I am still overweight on equities, as I believe global economic growth will resume and equities will provide a meaningful source of return, given proper diversification. In addition, the recent market pull-back has resulted in attractive valuation levels for stocks, which I see as an opportunity to invest.
The 10% cash buffer is consistent with the belief that attractive investment opportunities will continue to come our way in 2019.
Conclusion Despite strong expectations, 2018 marked a horrendous year for investors, as stocks gave away all the gains of the year in just a couple of months. However, the outlook for 2019 is not bleak, but investments should be made cautiously, as markets will remain volatile. In order to build a profitable portfolio despite this expected volatility, investors can stick to pre-set guidelines and invest in tranches.
